paragraphs: The SECOND point to be examined is whether the Convention was authorized to frame and propose this mixed Constitution.

Strictly speaking, the powers of the Convention should be determined by inspecting the commissions that the members received from their respective constituents. All of these commissions, however, referred either to the recommendation from the meeting at Annapolis in September, 1786, or to the one from Congress in February, 1787. It will therefore be enough to turn to these two acts.

The act from Annapolis recommends the "appointment of commissioners to take into consideration the situation of the United States; to devise SUCH FURTHER PROVISIONS as shall appear to them necessary to render the Constitution of the federal government ADEQUATE TO THE EXIGENCIES OF THE UNION; and to report such an act for that purpose, to the United States in Congress assembled, as when agreed to by them, and afterwards confirmed by the legislature of every State, will effectually provide for the same."

The act of Congress that made the recommendation reads as follows: "WHEREAS, There is provision in the articles of Confederation and perpetual Union, for making alterations therein, by the assent of a Congress of the United States, and of the legislatures of the several States; and whereas experience hath evinced, that there are defects in the present Confederation; as a mean to remedy which, several of the States, and PARTICULARLY THE STATE OF NEW YORK, by express instructions to their delegates in Congress, have suggested a convention for the purposes expressed in the following resolution; and such convention appearing to be the most probable mean of establishing in these States A FIRM NATIONAL GOVERNMENT:

"Resolved, That in the opinion of Congress it is expedient, that on the second Monday of May next a convention of delegates, who shall have been appointed by the several States, be held at Philadelphia, for the sole and express purpose OF REVISING THE ARTICLES OF CONFEDERATION, and reporting to Congress and the several legislatures such ALTERATIONS AND PROVISIONS THEREIN, as shall, when agreed to in Congress, and confirmed by the States, render the federal Constitution ADEQUATE TO THE EXIGENCIES OF GOVERNMENT AND THE PRESERVATION OF THE UNION."

The authority under which the Convention acted is to be drawn from comparing these several modes of expression and giving them a fair construction. The members were to frame a NATIONAL GOVERNMENT adequate to the EXIGENCIES OF GOVERNMENT, and OF THE UNION, and they were to reshape the articles of Confederation so as to accomplish these purposes.

There are two rules of construction, dictated by plain reason and also founded on legal axioms. The first is that every part of an expression should, if possible, be given some meaning and be made to work toward a common end. The second is that, where the several parts cannot be made to agree, the less important should give way to the more important; the means should be sacrificed to the end, rather than the end to the means.

Suppose, then, that the expressions defining the authority of the Convention were irreconcilably at odds with each other. Suppose that, in the Convention's judgment, a NATIONAL and ADEQUATE GOVERNMENT could not possibly be brought about by making ALTERATIONS and PROVISIONS in the ARTICLES OF CONFEDERATION. Which part of the definition should the Convention have embraced, and which should it have rejected? Which was the more important part, and which the less? Which was the end, and which the means? Let the most scrupulous interpreters of delegated powers, and the most determined objectors to the powers the Convention exercised, answer these questions. Let them declare whether it mattered more to the happiness of the people of America that the articles of Confederation be disregarded, an adequate government be provided and the Union be preserved, or that an adequate government be omitted and the articles of Confederation be preserved. Let them declare whether preserving these articles was the end, for the sake of which a reform of the government was to be introduced as the means; or whether the establishment of a government adequate to the national happiness was the end at which the articles themselves originally aimed, and to which they ought, as insufficient means, to have been sacrificed.

But is it necessary to suppose that these expressions are absolutely irreconcilable? Is it necessary to suppose that no ALTERATIONS or PROVISIONS in the articles of the confederation could possibly mold them into a national and adequate government, into such a government as the Convention has proposed?

No stress, it is presumed, will be laid on the TITLE in this case; changing it could never be deemed an exercise of ungranted power. ALTERATIONS in the body of the instrument are expressly authorized. NEW PROVISIONS in it are also expressly authorized. Here, then, is a power to change the title, to insert new articles and to alter old ones. Must it necessarily be admitted that this power is exceeded so long as any part of the old articles remains? Those who maintain that it must should at least mark the boundary between authorized and usurped innovations: between the degree of change that lies within the compass of ALTERATIONS AND FURTHER PROVISIONS, and the degree that amounts to a TRANSMUTATION of the government. Will it be said that the alterations ought not to have touched the substance of the Confederation? The States would never have appointed a convention with so much solemnity, nor described its objects so broadly, if they had not had some SUBSTANTIAL reform in mind. Will it be said that the FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES of the Confederation were not within the purview of the Convention, and ought not to have been varied? I ask, What are these principles? Do they require that, in establishing the Constitution, the States should be regarded as distinct and independent sovereigns? The proposed Constitution regards them in just that way. Do they require that the members of the government should derive their appointment from the legislatures, not from the people of the States? One branch of the new government is to be appointed by these legislatures; and under the Confederation the delegates to Congress MAY ALL be appointed directly by the people, and in two States(1) they actually are. Do they require that the powers of the government should act on the States, and not directly on individuals? In some instances, as has been shown, the powers of the new government will act on the States in their collective characters. In some instances, also, the powers of the existing government act directly on individuals. In cases of capture; of piracy; of the post office; of coins, weights, and measures; of trade with the Indians; of claims under grants of land by different States; and, above all, in the case of trials by courts-martial in the army and navy, by which death may be inflicted without the intervention of a jury, or even of a civil magistrate; in all these cases the powers of the Confederation operate directly on the persons and interests of individual citizens. Do these fundamental principles require, in particular, that no tax be levied without the intermediate agency of the States? The Confederation itself authorizes a direct tax, to a certain extent, on the post office. Congress has also construed the power of coinage so as to levy a tribute directly from that source. But setting these instances aside, was it not an acknowledged object of the Convention, and the universal expectation of the people, that the regulation of trade should be submitted to the general government in such a form as to make it a direct source of general revenue? Had not Congress repeatedly recommended this measure as not inconsistent with the fundamental principles of the Confederation? Had not every State but one, and New York herself among them, gone far enough along with the plan of Congress to recognize the PRINCIPLE of the innovation? Do these principles, in short, require that the powers of the general government be limited, and that beyond this limit the States be left in possession of their sovereignty and independence? We have seen that in the new government, as in the old, the general powers are limited, and that the States, in all unenumerated cases, are left in the enjoyment of their sovereign and independent jurisdiction.

The truth is that the great principles of the Constitution proposed by the Convention may be considered less as absolutely new than as an expansion of principles found in the articles of Confederation. The misfortune under the latter system has been that these principles are so feeble and confined that they justify all the charges of ineffectiveness brought against it, and require so much enlargement that the new system has the look of an entire transformation of the old.

In one particular it is admitted that the Convention has departed from the terms of its commission. Instead of reporting a plan that requires the confirmation OF THE LEGISLATURES OF ALL THE STATES, it has reported a plan that is to be confirmed by the PEOPLE and may be put into effect by NINE STATES ONLY. It is worth remarking that this objection, though the most plausible, has been the least pressed in the publications that have swarmed against the Convention. The restraint can only have come from an irresistible conviction of the absurdity of subjecting the fate of twelve States to the perverseness or corruption of a thirteenth. It can also have come from the example of inflexible opposition given by a MAJORITY of one sixtieth of the people of America to a measure approved and called for by the voice of twelve States, comprising fifty-nine sixtieths of the people. That example is still fresh in the memory and indignation of every citizen who has felt for the wounded honor and prosperity of his country. Since those who have criticized the powers of the Convention have in a manner waived this objection, I dismiss it without further comment.
The THIRD point to be inquired into is how far considerations of duty arising out of the case itself could have made up for any defect of regular authority.

In the preceding inquiries the powers of the Convention have been analyzed and tested with the same rigor, and by the same rules, as if they had been real and final powers to establish a Constitution for the United States. We have seen how they have stood the test even on that supposition. It is time now to recall that the powers were merely advisory and recommendatory; that the States meant them so, and the Convention understood them so; and that the Convention has accordingly planned and proposed a Constitution that will be of no more consequence than the paper it is written on, unless it is stamped with the approval of those to whom it is addressed. This reflection puts the subject in an altogether different light, and will enable us to judge properly the course the Convention took.

Let us look at the ground on which the Convention stood. It may be gathered from their proceedings that they were deeply and unanimously impressed with the crisis that had led their country, almost with one voice, to make so singular and solemn an experiment in correcting the errors of a system that had produced this crisis. They were no less deeply and unanimously convinced that such a reform as they have proposed was absolutely necessary to accomplish the purposes of their appointment. They could not have been unaware that the hopes and expectations of the great body of citizens throughout this great empire were turned, with the keenest anxiety, to the outcome of their deliberations. They had every reason to believe that opposite feelings agitated the minds and hearts of every external and internal enemy of the liberty and prosperity of the United States. They had seen, in the origin and progress of the experiment, the eagerness with which the PROPOSITION made by a single State (Virginia), toward a partial amendment of the Confederation, had been taken up and promoted. They had seen the LIBERTY ASSUMED by a VERY FEW deputies from a VERY FEW States, meeting at Annapolis, of recommending a great and critical object wholly foreign to their commission, not only justified by public opinion but actually carried into effect by twelve out of the thirteen States. They had seen, in a variety of instances, Congress assume not only recommendatory but operative powers, which the public judged to be warranted by occasions and objects infinitely less urgent than those that were to govern their own conduct. They must have reflected that in all great changes of established governments, forms ought to give way to substance; that a rigid adherence to forms in such cases would make nominal and worthless the transcendent and precious right of the people to "abolish or alter their governments as to them shall seem most likely to effect their safety and happiness,"(2) since it is impossible for the people spontaneously and universally to move in concert toward their object; and that it is therefore essential that such changes be set in motion by some INFORMAL AND UNAUTHORIZED PROPOSITIONS, made by some patriotic and respectable citizen or number of citizens. They must have recalled that it was by this irregular and assumed privilege of proposing to the people plans for their safety and happiness that the States were first united against the danger with which their ancient government threatened them; that committees and congresses were formed to concentrate their efforts and defend their rights; and that CONVENTIONS were ELECTED in THE SEVERAL STATES to establish the constitutions under which they are now governed. Nor could they have forgotten that no petty, ill-timed scruples, no zeal for adhering to ordinary forms, were seen anywhere, except in those who wished to indulge, under these masks, their secret enmity to the substance being contended for. They must have borne in mind that, since the plan to be framed and proposed was to be submitted TO THE PEOPLE THEMSELVES, the disapproval of this supreme authority would destroy it forever, while its approval would blot out earlier errors and irregularities. It might even have occurred to them that, where a disposition to cavil prevailed, their neglect to use the degree of power vested in them, and still more their recommending any measure whatever not warranted by their commission, would draw no less criticism than a recommendation, all at once, of a measure fully equal to the national exigencies.

Suppose the Convention, under all these impressions and in the midst of all these considerations, had not shown a manly confidence in its country, by whose confidence it had been so particularly distinguished, and had not pointed out a system capable, in its judgment, of securing the country's happiness. Suppose it had instead taken the cold and sullen resolution of disappointing the country's ardent hopes, of sacrificing substance to forms, of committing the dearest interests of the country to the uncertainties of delay and the hazard of events. Let me ask the man who can raise his mind to one elevated conception, who can awaken in his heart one patriotic emotion, what judgment the impartial world, the friends of mankind and every virtuous citizen ought to have pronounced on the conduct and character of this assembly. Or if there is a man whose inclination to condemn is susceptible of no control, let me ask what sentence he has in reserve for the twelve States who USURPED THE POWER of sending deputies to the Convention, a body utterly unknown to their constitutions; for Congress, who recommended the appointment of this body, equally unknown to the Confederation; and for the State of New York in particular, which first urged this unauthorized interposition and then complied with it.

But so that the objectors may be disarmed of every pretext, let it be granted for a moment that the Convention was neither authorized by its commission nor justified by circumstances in proposing a Constitution for its country. Does it follow that the Constitution ought, for that reason alone, to be rejected? If, according to the noble precept, it is lawful to accept good advice even from an enemy, shall we set the ignoble example of refusing such advice even when our friends offer it? The prudent question in all cases should surely be not so much FROM WHOM the advice comes as whether the advice is GOOD.

The sum of what has been advanced and proved here is this. The charge against the Convention of exceeding its powers has no foundation to support it, except in one instance that the objectors have little pressed. If the Convention had exceeded its powers, it was not only warranted but required, as the confidential servant of its country, by the circumstances in which it was placed, to use the liberty it assumed. And finally, if it had violated both its powers and its obligations in proposing a Constitution, this Constitution ought nevertheless to be embraced if it is calculated to accomplish the views and happiness of the people of America. How far the Constitution deserves this description is the subject under investigation.
